backTranslations.41: **Before the visit** - Add the date of your doctor visit on the Visit tab. MenoMap shows how complete your notes are and what would improve them. Pick the topics and questions that matter most; stick to three or four. Create your notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date. **During the visit** - Hand over or show the first page. It is made to be read in under a minute: counts, averages, the heat calendar and your questions. Start with the question that matters most to you. If your doctor speaks another language you can create the notes in that language. **What the notes are, and are not** - They are a summary of what you have recorded, plus what you chose to pull from the Health app. They are not a diagnosis and not a complete medical record, and any patterns in them are a coincidence check, not proof of a cause. Your doctor may ask questions the notes cannot answer, and that is normal. **After the visit** - Add new medications with start dates. In a few weeks MenoMap can show your entries before and after, which makes the next follow-up easier.
backTranslations.42: **Menopause** is a single point in time: the day when 12 months in a row have passed without a period, when this is not explained by something else (such as pregnancy, certain medications or an operation). In many countries it occurs on average in the early 50s, but anything from the mid 40s to the mid 50s is common. **Perimenopause** is the years leading up to that point. Hormone levels rise and fall unevenly, so periods can become irregular, heavier, lighter, more frequent or less frequent. Many of the changes associated with the change of life (klimakteriet), such as hot flashes, night sweats, changed sleep and changed mood, often begin here, while periods still come. Perimenopause can last a few years or considerably longer, and it looks different for everyone. **Postmenopause** is everything after that 12-month mark. Some symptoms settle over time; others can continue for several years. Menopause can also come earlier because of an operation in which the ovaries are removed, certain cancer treatments or other conditions. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency, and it is worth raising with a doctor. **How it is established.** For many people over 45, the doctor can establish perimenopause or menopause from your medical history and symptoms. Blood tests are not always needed, since hormone levels swing from day to day. They are more often used when someone is younger or when the picture is unclear. **What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell which stage you are in. What MenoMap can do is keep an honest log of what you notice: waves, sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and your doctor can look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162: Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden wave of heat, often in the face, neck and chest, sometimes with flushing, sweating, palpitations or chills afterwards. A night sweat is the same thing during sleep, and it can be so heavy that you wake up or the sheets get soaked. They are among the most common changes around menopause. Some have a few mild ones; others have many a day that disturb work and sleep. For some they fade within a few years; for others they last much longer. **What can make them more likely.** Many notice patterns with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, warm rooms, stress or thick bedding. It varies a lot from person to person, and therefore following your own tags can be more useful than a general list. **There are other causes.** Flushing and sweating can also be due to thyroid problems, infections, certain medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not fit the usual pattern, or come together with weight loss, fever or a feeling of being ill, raise it with a doctor. **Describing them well.** Useful details before a visit: roughly how many per day and per night; how strong they feel and how long they last; what they interrupt: sleep, work, conversation, exercise; what seems to come before them; what you have tried, and whether it changed anything. MenoMap's Wave button and the after-the-fact log exist to capture exactly this without much effort. **Help exists.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatments, plus practical ways to handle the symptoms. Which ones suit you is something to talk about with a doctor.

backTranslations.291: Hormone therapy (often called MHT or HRT) replaces some of the estrogen that the body makes less of around menopause. Major guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats for many, and it can help with other symptoms too. **It comes in different forms:** patches, gel, spray, tablets and low-dose vaginal preparations for local symptoms such as dryness. Someone who still has a uterus usually gets progestogen together with the estrogen to protect the lining of the uterus. **Benefits and risks depend on the person:** age, how long since periods stopped, own and family medical history (for example breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease) and the type of treatment and how it is taken. Therefore it is a decision to make together with a doctor who knows your history, not something an app can decide. **Questions many ask:** Is hormone therapy an option for me, and why or why not? Which type and form would you suggest, and why? What benefit can I expect, and how soon? What are my personal risks, and how do they compare with not treating? What should I watch for, and when should we follow up? **If you already take it,** log it in MenoMap (You -> Medications). MenoMap shows your waves before and after you started, as a coincidence check and not as proof, so that you have something concrete to bring up at the follow-up. MenoMap never suggests that you start, stop or change a medication.

backTranslations.293: Hormone therapy does not suit everyone, and some simply prefer other paths. There are several. **Prescription options.** Some non-hormonal medications have scientific support for reducing hot flashes. These include certain medications originally developed for other conditions, and a newer group developed specifically against hot flashes. Each has its own benefit, its own side effects and interactions, so a doctor can help you weigh them against each other. **Talking and mind-body methods.** Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) adapted for menopause has scientific support for making hot flashes and night sweats less bothersome and for improving sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied. **Practical changes many benefit from:** layers you can quickly take off; a fan at the desk and at the bed; a cooler bedroom and breathable bedding; noticing and reducing your personal triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments help here); regular physical activity and fixed sleep routines. **Dietary supplements and herbal products.** The scientific support is mixed or limited for many of them, quality varies and some interact with other medications. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about everything you take, including over-the-counter products. **Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiment compares your own records before and during a change, which is easier to judge than a feeling.

The app does not diagnose menopause or any other diagnosis, does not prescribe or change treatment and does not replace care from a qualified doctor. backTranslations.416: Most doctor visits are short, and it is hard to remember a month of nights offhand. People tend to remember the last days or the worst ones. A simple log fills the gap. **Here is what a diary gives your doctor:** how often the symptoms come and how strong they are, not just that they exist; whether it is getting better, worse or unchanged; what was going on around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medications; a starting point to compare against if you try a treatment. **Keep it simple.** A diary only helps if you keep it. MenoMap is built around a one-tap Wave button and a four-question evening check-in, so it takes seconds, not a whole notepad. **Two weeks is a good start.** Two to four weeks of records usually give a clearer picture than a single bad week. **Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid, and things that worry you. MenoMap's Visit tab helps you choose questions and prints them with your notes.

backTranslations.479: When 12 months have passed without a period, **all bleeding from the vagina should be examined by a doctor**, even if it only happened once, and even if it was only spotting or light pink or brownish discharge. Most often the cause turns out not to be serious. For example, it is common for the lining of the vagina or uterus to become thinner. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat when found early. Therefore public health advice says to have it examined rather than wait. **If you take hormone therapy** some bleeding patterns can be expected, depending on which type you take. Bleeding that is unexpected for your treatment, heavier than usual or that comes at the wrong time should also be examined. **Here is what to do:** Contact your doctor or the health service and say that you have had a bleed after menopause. Note the date, how much and anything else you noticed. MenoMap can save it for you (You -> Menstrual cycle). MenoMap cannot say why the bleeding occurred. The app reminds you to have it examined and includes it in your notes for the visit.

backTranslations.529: Poor sleep is one of the most common complaints in midlife, and it rarely has a single cause. **Night sweats** can wake you straight away, or make you too warm or damp to settle again. **Other common contributing causes:** needing to pee at night; anxiety or racing thoughts; alcohol, which can help you fall asleep but often makes the second half of the night more fragmented; caffeine later in the day; pain, restless legs or a partner who snores; snoring or breathing pauses, which can be a sign of sleep apnea (worth raising, especially if you are very sleepy in the daytime). **This tends to help.** A cool, dark room; breathable bedding and layers you can take off; a fixed wake-up time; and less alcohol near bedtime. CBT for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured and well-studied method, and many doctors can refer you there. **What you can track.** For a week or two, note your sleep score, waves at night, alcohol and late caffeine. MenoMap's evening check-in and the wave log do this with a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show your sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app next to your night sweats, as context rather than as an explanation. **When you should seek care.** Talk to a doctor if poor sleep affects your safety (for example when driving), your mood or your daily life, or if you notice breathing pauses or gasping for air at night.
